prompt: A capable team starts rewriting Coleta from scratch. Why does the lesson expect the new system to fall behind the old one?
hint: Look at what happened to Coleta in the last twelve months.

choices.text: RPG is too hard for programmers who learnt modern languages to read
choices.why: Reading RPG is a skill people learn; the lesson's problem is not the language but a target that changes while it is copied.

choices.text: Coleta keeps changing, so each change is made twice
choices.why: Right: 23 changes in a year, each needed in Coleta for today's payments and in the copy for the day it takes over, and the copy falls behind.

choices.text: Its database is too large to copy into a modern system in one go
choices.why: Volume is a data-migration question for lesson 14, and Coleta's data is not large; the rewrite falls behind because the rules keep moving.

choices.text: A new system is slower to build than the original was
choices.why: Speed of building is not the argument; a fast team copying a moving system still ends up copying the wrong version.

prompt: In a big-bang replacement of Coleta, when is the new payment calculation first proved against real farms?
hint: Think about where the risk in the figure is released.

choices.text: In the acceptance tests, which are run against a copy of real farms' data
choices.why: A copy of the data in a test proves the cases somebody thought of; real farms, with their phone calls and bank accounts, arrive on payment day.

choices.text: At each sprint review, when a finished feature is demonstrated
choices.why: A demonstration shows a feature working on prepared data; in a big bang nothing reaches a farm until the cutover.

choices.text: On the first payment day after cutover, for all 1,900 at once
choices.why: Right: that is the whole problem of the big bang, everything proved on one day, and payments already made are hard to take back.

choices.text: When Coleta is switched off, some weeks after the cutover
choices.why: By the time the old system is off, the new one has already paid the farms; the proof came on the first payment day, not later.

prompt: Serra Alta's plant-visit booking tool is used by ten people, holds about 400 bookings, has rules nobody has changed in years, and no other system calls it. It is being replaced. What fits the lesson?
hint: The strangler has a price; check what it buys here.

choices.text: Strangle it all the same: a big bang is a known way to fail
choices.why: The big bang fails for reasons this tool does not have: no moving target, no hidden rules, nothing calling it, no money moving.

choices.text: Replace it in one go and check the data by hand
choices.why: Yes: small, frozen and called by nobody, so coexistence would cost more than the risk it removes.

choices.text: Run old and new side by side for three months and compare every booking
choices.why: A parallel run protects a calculation that moves money; for 400 bookings it is months of effort to check what a person checks in an afternoon.

choices.text: Put a facade in front first, so the tool could be routed later
choices.why: A facade earns its place when callers have to be moved without noticing; this tool has no callers to move.

prompt: Which of these are reasons the lesson gives for big-bang rewrites failing in a company like Serra Alta? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three reasons are built into the shape of a big bang.

choices.text: The old system changes while it is being copied
choices.why: Yes: the target moves, and the copy falls behind it.

choices.text: Old languages like RPG lack features the business needs
choices.why: Coleta's rules work; what is missing is a written statement of them, not a language feature.

choices.text: The full rules exist only in the code
choices.why: Yes: the manual covers the main formula and none of the exceptions.

choices.text: Every risk is proved on one cutover date
choices.why: Yes: nothing is proved until then, and then everything is.

choices.text: Rewritten systems need more servers than the old ones
choices.why: Infrastructure size is not one of the three reasons, and it says nothing about whether the new system pays farms correctly.

prompt: A team proposes replacing Coleta in three steps: its data to a new database first, then its logic into services, then its screens. What does the lesson say about that plan?
hint: Ask when the first thing a caller asks for is served by the new side.

choices.text: It is the safest order, since the data is what everything else stands on
choices.why: Moving the data first sounds like laying a foundation, but no capability works on the new side until the screens move too.

choices.text: It works if each of the three steps is done over a single weekend
choices.why: Short steps do not help when each one leaves a halfway state that serves nobody; the risk still lands when the last step is done.

choices.text: It is a strangler as long as a facade stands in front
choices.why: A facade with nothing to route to is decoration; the strangler moves capabilities, and this plan moves none until the end.

choices.text: Nothing is served by the new side until the last layer moves
choices.why: Right: slicing by layer is a big bang in disguise, with all the risk retired at the end.

prompt: Coleta stores some farms' tank sizes wrongly. Rui's team offers to correct them inside the farm-lookup flow on the bus, since every lookup passes through it. What does the lesson advise?
hint: One of the four rules for the facade.

choices.text: Decline: the facade routes, and the fix goes where the data is owned
choices.why: Yes: a facade that corrects data becomes a third system with rules of its own, which then has to be migrated too.

choices.text: Accept: the facade sees every request, so it is the cheapest place
choices.why: Cheap today, and it leaves a rule nobody will look for in a routing layer when Coleta is switched off.

choices.text: Accept, provided each correction is written to the log
choices.why: Logging makes the rule visible but does not take it out of the facade; it is still business logic in the wrong place.

choices.text: Decline, because the bus will be gone before long anyway
choices.why: The bus may well outlive Coleta; the reason to decline is what the facade is for, not how long it will last.

prompt: Put one turn of the strangler in the lesson's order, for a system that has a front door.
hint: The facade comes before anything moves, and removal comes last.
items: Put a facade in front of the legacy, passing everything through
Build that capability end to end in the new system
Route the capability to the new system, keeping a way back
Remove the capability from the legacy
trap: Removing the capability from the legacy before its route has proved itself throws away the cheap undo the facade exists to give.

prompt: Where does Coleta already have something that works as a facade?
hint: Where does another system ask Coleta a question and wait?

choices.text: In the green-screen menus the six clerks use
choices.why: The clerks type straight into Coleta; nothing stands between them and it, which is why the screens move with the people.

choices.text: In the nightly file SAP loads
choices.why: That file is an output, and the plan keeps its format as a contract; it does not route requests to anybody.

choices.text: In the two bus flows called by Rota and the quality dashboard
choices.why: Correct: the callers talk to the bus and only the bus knows the answer comes from RPG, so a flow's destination changes and nobody else does.

choices.text: In the folder on the IBM i where the handheld files arrive
choices.why: A folder receives files and answers nobody; reaching that flow takes interception, the next section's technique.

prompt: Match each technique to the situation the lesson uses it for.
hint: Ask where the work enters and who owns the code.

pairs.right: work arrives as a file you can stand in the path of
changes are typed into the legacy's own screens
deciding which one kind of entity changes owner first
the caller is code your own team releases

right_distractors: every caller already goes through an HTTP proxy

prompt: Why were the laboratory results Joana's first asset to capture?
hint: Four reasons, and the first two are about how the data moves.

choices.text: They are the largest data set, so moving them first retires the most risk
choices.why: Size is not the criterion; a large first slice is the opposite of a slice chosen to teach.

choices.text: The payment does not use them, so a mistake there costs nothing
choices.why: The payment does use them; that is why a translated copy goes back to Coleta every evening.

choices.text: One outside file a day, and no screen in Coleta edits them
choices.why: Right: easy to intercept and nothing to synchronise back, plus Coleta uses them in one place and the quality team wants them sooner.

choices.text: They are the oldest data in Coleta and the most likely to be wrong
choices.why: Age and quality are profiling questions for lesson 14; the choice here was about how the data enters and who changes it.

prompt: Change data capture delivers this from Coleta's journal: farm 041327, status `A` → `S`, 14:02. What does the new side know from that row alone?
hint: CDC gives rows, not intentions.

choices.text: That the farm was suspended for quality, since that is what S stands for
choices.why: S has meant two things since 2014; without the remark, quality and a missing document look identical.

choices.text: That the status changed then, and not why
choices.why: Yes: the journal records what changed and when; what it means is the anti-corruption layer's inference, and it needs the remark.

choices.text: That a clerk made the change at a terminal
choices.why: The journal names a program, not a person's reason; a batch job writes to the same table, so even who did it is an inference.

choices.text: Nothing at all, as CDC only reports tables the new side already owns
choices.why: CDC reads the legacy's tables precisely because the legacy owns them; that is what makes it useful in the middle of a migration.

prompt: Rota's team wants to switch its route planner between farm lookup on the bus and the new farm service, and back, while both exist. Which approach does the lesson describe?
hint: Their own codebase, released from the main branch.

choices.text: A long-lived branch with the new calls, merged on the cutover day
choices.why: A long-lived branch is exactly what branch by abstraction avoids: the switch happens in released code, behind a flag.

choices.text: Ask Sebastião to make Coleta call the new service
choices.why: Changing Coleta is what the migration keeps to a minimum, and its one safe author is leaving.

choices.text: Copy the new service's farms into Rota's own database every night
choices.why: A nightly copy makes a third place holding farms and a sync to maintain, and switching back means another copy.

choices.text: An interface with both implementations behind a flag
choices.why: Right: branch by abstraction, the facade's idea moved inside one program, releasable at every step.

prompt: What is the anti-corruption layer for?
hint: Evans's description: isolating, in both directions.

choices.text: Blocking damaged records from the legacy before they reach the network
choices.why: It does refuse what it cannot read, but its purpose is the model, not the network; the corruption it prevents is of the new design.

choices.text: Translating at the border, so the new model keeps its own terms
choices.why: Right: the legacy's codes and formats stop at the layer, and the new system is not built in Coleta's shape.

choices.text: Encrypting what passes between the old system and the new
choices.why: Encryption protects data in transit; it changes nothing about which model the new system is built on.

choices.text: Checking each morning that both systems hold the same totals
choices.why: That is the morning reconciliation, from the coexistence section; it compares totals and translates nothing.

prompt: In Coleta's `CYYMMDD` form, the value `1261023` is 23 October ___.
hint: The leading digit is the century: 0 for the 1900s, 1 for the 2000s.

prompt: Coleta stores a volume of milk as a whole number of hundredths of a litre. A collection is stored as `84275`. How many litres is it?
hint: Divide by one hundred.

prompt: To avoid writing a translation, the new team asks Sebastião to change Coleta so it stores ISO dates and plain litres. What does the lesson say?
hint: Whose side does the layer sit on, and why?

choices.text: Yes: fixing the source once is cheaper than translating for years
choices.why: It would be, for a system with a future; Coleta is being switched off, and every change to it is a risk taken with the person who is leaving.

choices.text: Yes, provided a parallel run proves the change first
choices.why: A parallel run protects a calculation that changes; the lesson's point is to avoid changing Coleta at all, not to test the change.

choices.text: No: the new side owns the layer, so Coleta stays as it is
choices.why: Right: the side that wants to stay clean pays for the translation, and the legacy is not touched while its expert leaves.

choices.text: No, because IBM i has no way to store an ISO date
choices.why: The platform's database has a date type; the reason not to change Coleta is risk and ownership, not a limit of IBM i.

prompt: In phase 2, someone proposes that the new correction screen should also call a Coleta program directly, so Coleta gets each correction at once. What is the problem?
hint: Two systems, two writes, no shared transaction.

choices.text: If one write fails after the other succeeds, the two disagree silently
choices.why: Right: the clerk sees a saved correction, Coleta never got it, and a farmer finds out weeks later.

choices.text: It doubles the load on Coleta's database
choices.why: One more call per correction is no load at all; the danger is the failure in the middle, not the volume.

choices.text: The clerks would have to type every correction twice
choices.why: The proposal is one screen writing to both systems; nobody types twice, which is why it looks harmless.

choices.text: Coleta would hold the correction before the master did
choices.why: The order is not the issue; even in the right order, a failed second write leaves the two apart with nothing to say so.

prompt: In the first month of the shadow calculation, 1,871 of 1,900 farms were identical to the centavo. What percentage was identical, to one decimal place?
hint: Identical farms divided by all farms, times 100.

prompt: 17 farms differed only by rounding, none by more than six centavos. A developer suggests a tolerance of ten centavos so the comparison passes. What does the lesson do instead?
hint: A tolerance hides a fact about two methods.

choices.text: Accepts the tolerance, as six centavos never matter to a farm
choices.why: Farmers compare statements month to month; and the tolerance would hide that the two calculations work differently.

choices.text: Keeps the new method, since rounding once is more exact
choices.why: It may be the better method, but changing it silently is what the decision avoided; a change of method is announced.

choices.text: Leaves the 17 out of the comparison as noise
choices.why: Excluding them is a tolerance by another name; every difference was explained, not removed.

choices.text: Has someone with authority decide which result is right
choices.why: Right: Marcos decided the replacement rounds per collection, like Coleta, and the comparison stays exact to the centavo.

prompt: It is phase 2. A clerk notices yesterday's litres for a farm are wrong and opens Coleta's collection screen to fix them. What happens, according to the master table?
hint: Who is master of daily collections from September 2027?

choices.text: Coleta accepts it, and the copy carries it across to the new system
choices.why: Copies flow one way, from the master; in phase 2 the master of collections is the new system, so the copy runs the other way.

choices.text: It is refused there; the fix belongs in the new system
choices.why: Right: the new system is master of collections from phase 2, and the old screen stopped accepting changes on that date.

choices.text: Both systems accept it and the morning reconciliation settles the difference
choices.why: Reconciliation finds drift between a master and its copy; it is not a way of choosing between two masters.

choices.text: The fix goes to SAP, which holds the farm's vendor record
choices.why: SAP holds the vendor and bank account, not the litres; collections are Coleta's and then the new system's.

prompt: Nine capabilities have moved. The first inventory listed 12; the search found 3 more. What percentage of the real total has moved?
hint: The denominator is the inventory after the search.

prompt: Put the steps for switching Coleta off in the lesson's order.
hint: Each step is reversible until the one where going back stops being cheap.
items: End the contracts and everything around it
trap: Ending the contracts before the machine has been off for the agreed period removes the last cheap way back.

prompt: How did Joana's team find the three capabilities that were in no inventory?
hint: The system keeps evidence of who uses it.

choices.text: By asking each department head to list what they use
choices.why: Asking finds what people remember; a spreadsheet nobody calls a system and a February job are what they forget.

choices.text: By switching the IBM i off for a weekend and waiting for complaints
choices.why: That finds users as incidents, and a weekend would never have found a job that runs once a year.

choices.text: By listing every flow on the bus that names Coleta
choices.why: The bus knew about two flows; the spreadsheet used ODBC and the cooperative file left by the scheduler, outside the bus.

choices.text: By reading a year of scheduler history and the database connections
choices.why: Right: the system's own evidence names its users, whoever thought to mention them, months before a read-only period.

prompt: A monthly report says: "Migration 80% complete: 12 of 15 capabilities live in the new systems." Coleta still runs, its contracts renew, and its jobs still start every night. What is the best reading?
hint: Two counts, and the report shows one.

choices.text: The work is nearly done, so the switch-off can be set for next month
choices.why: The date belongs in a decision record from the start; and with three capabilities still in Coleta, nothing yet says it can stop.

choices.text: The new side is capable, but nothing is switched off yet
choices.why: Right: progress is measured by what was switched off, and here that count is still at zero.

choices.text: The figure is wrong because capabilities should be weighted by size
choices.why: Weighting changes the first count's arithmetic, not what it measures; it still counts what was built.

choices.text: The report is sound as long as the parallel run has ended
choices.why: The parallel run protects one capability's correctness; it says nothing about what the company still depends on.

prompt: Phase 3 moves the farm register to the new system. Which of these belong in that move? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ownership, translation, and what does not move.

choices.text: Make the new system master on one date, and stop Coleta's register screen accepting changes that day
choices.why: Yes: a change of master happens on a phase's date, for the whole kind of data, and the old screen stops that day.

choices.text: Let both systems accept edits for a month, so the clerks get used to the new one
choices.why: Two places accepting changes is two masters, and they will disagree with nobody able to say which is right.

choices.text: Read status `S` with its remark, in the anti-corruption layer
choices.why: Yes: S means two things, and the layer is where the remark decides which.

choices.text: Bring the farms' bank accounts from SAP into the new register
choices.why: The farms are vendors in SAP, which holds their bank accounts in every phase; that row of the table never moves.

choices.text: Write the register's rules from Coleta's 2003 manual
choices.why: The manual covers the main formula and none of the exceptions; the rules come from Coleta's behaviour, written as tests with Sebastião.

prompt: A different company's legacy warehouse system has an HTTP API that every caller uses, and its data changes only through that API. Which technique carries a strangler there?
hint: Is there a front door this time?

choices.text: Change data capture on its database, as with any legacy
choices.why: CDC is for changes that bypass any interface you can stand in; here every change passes through the API.

choices.text: Interception of the files it receives each night
choices.why: This system takes its work through an API, not through files; there is no file path to stand in.

choices.text: A routing facade in front of the API, one capability at a time
choices.why: Right: this is the textbook case, a front door every request passes through, routed by capability.

choices.text: A big bang, since an API makes the switch a single change
choices.why: An easy switch does not prove the new system; the risk of one date carrying everything is the same.
